newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Surgeon says Yeltsin heart operation may be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Surgeon says Yeltsin heart operation may be delayed.

text.p: A Russian surgeon, chosen to carry out heart surgery on President Boris Yeltsin, said in a television interview shown on Sunday that the operation could be delayed by up to two months judging by the patient's condition.

Renat Akchurin told NTV commercial television that a group of Russian and foreign doctors was due to decide on Wednesday or Thursday when to hold a bypass surgery to improve blood supply to Yeltsin's heart and whether the operation was was generally safe for the patient.
"We will see how the patient is prepared for the operation," said Akchurin, who said he would head the team of 12 surgeons if the operation takes place.
"Any risk should be justified. If the risk is justified go and do the operation. If it is not, don't do silly things."
Asked by Yevgeny Kiselyov, an anchorman of NTV's weekly show Itogi, when the operation would take place, Akchurin, answered: "Within 1-1/2 or two months."
As doctors mulled medical aspects of the planned surgery, politicians looked into its possible political consequences.
Presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais warned Yeltsin's political rivals on Saturday against trying to try to step into 65-year-old Yeltsin's shoes.

"Those politicians who believe that it is time to take up starting positions in a presidential campaign will very soon realise that they have jumped the gun," he told a congress of the Russia's Democratic Choice party in Moscow.
A decree issued on Thursday confirmed that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, would govern while the president was incapacitated.
But the Kremlin leader appeared reluctant to loosen his grip on power for any substential period of time.
Kremlin sources have said that Yeltsin was likely to transfer his powers, including a control over the "nuclear button", only for a few hours while he is unconscious in the operation theatre.
He appeared even less inclined to allow doctors to drop plans for the operation.
Asked whether the operation could be dropped for good, Akchurin answered: "It is possible but special conditions should be created for the president then.
"We would be forced to limit his physical activies. He is not going to tolerate this."
Akchurin, in unusually open remarks, told Reuters on Saturday it might be too dangerous to go ahead with the planned bypass surgery, but added he hoped it would still be possible.
The presidential press office issued no statements and could not be reached for comment, despite a newly-declared policy of openness.

Russian media treated the comments with caution, carrying them without fanfare. Even the opposition communists did not respond, saying only that party leader Gennady Zyuganov had left on a trip to the Council of Europe in Strasbourg.
Yeltsin disapeared from public eyes in late June, right in the middle of his vigorous re-election campaign which had finally brought him a second term in the Kremlin.

Yeltsin aides have long insisted that the president, who has a history of heart problems, was all right, just overtired. Yeltsin was reported to have taken a holiday at Zavidovo residence outside Moscow and later at Rus hunting lodge.
Earlier this month, Yeltsin said in a televised interview that he needed heart surgery and that he had agreed to undergo it. Yeltsin said the operation was likely in late September.
Akchurin appeared quite critical about the way Yeltsin was handled while in Zavidovo.
"I saw Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) two or three weeks ago," he said. "We have looked at results of his Zavdovo period.
"I cannot say I was too pleased with this results. He was tiring himself, hunting, fishing. This is not something we can reccomend for this sort of patient."
He made clear he was not in favour of early operation.

"We need to go throught a certain preparatory period and Boris Nikolayvich, who whips us up all the time, seems to understand this," Akchurin said. "An earlier date of the operation means bigger risks."
